title: GLP-1 Drugs Carry a Small but Real Hair-Loss Signal
hook: Anecdotes about thinning hair on Ozempic and Mounjaro now have data behind them: a BMJ study found a higher rate of hair loss than with two other diabetes drug classes. The good news is which kind.
key_points: Researchers compared roughly 12,000 GLP-1 users (semaglutide, tirzepatide) with users of SGLT-2 and DPP-4 inhibitors in health records from 2019–2024.
Hair loss ran 37% higher than with SGLT-2 inhibitors (6.91 vs 5.04 per 1,000 person-years) and 68% higher than with DPP-4 inhibitors (6.53 vs 3.89).
Absolute risk stayed low either way — roughly 5–7 cases per 1,000 person-years.
The excess was in non-scarring alopecia, where the follicle survives, so regrowth is possible.
Records lacked detail on the severity, extent, or duration of the hair loss.
It's observational: rapid weight loss itself can trigger shedding, so the drug may not be the whole story.
content_html: If you've seen people on Ozempic or Mounjaro mention thinning hair, that anecdote now has a study behind it. Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania Health System combed electronic health records from January 2019 through September 2024 and compared people with type 2 diabetes taking GLP-1 drugs — semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) — against people taking two other diabetes drug classes.
extra_html:
The GLP-1 group had more hair loss both ways it was measured. Against about 15,000 SGLT-2 inhibitor users, the roughly 12,000 GLP-1 users had a 37% higher rate — 6.91 versus 5.04 cases per 1,000 person-years. Against DPP-4 inhibitor users, the gap was 68% (6.53 versus 3.89). Narrowing to non-scarring alopecia specifically, the excess was 53% and 72%. Published in The BMJ, the authors framed it modestly: "Our findings extend previous anecdotal safety signals and provide more systematic evidence to inform clinical awareness of this potential adverse effect."

Two things keep this in proportion. First, the absolute numbers are small — five to seven cases per 1,000 person-years — and the excess was in non-scarring alopecia, meaning the follicles survive and hair can come back. The researchers noted their records "did not provide enough detail to determine the severity, extent, or duration of the alopecia." Second, this is observational. GLP-1 users in the study were younger and heavier than the comparison groups, and rapid weight loss from any cause is itself a known trigger for shedding, so the drug may be a marker as much as a cause. If you're on one of these drugs and noticing hair loss, it's worth raising with your prescriber rather than quietly stopping the medication.

related.title: The Ozempic and Wegovy Mistake Sending Thousands to Poison Control
related.hook: Poison control calls about semaglutide (Ozempic and Wegovy) have soared — not from misuse, but from simple dosing mistakes that basic education could largely prevent.

related.title: GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Lower Addiction Risk
related.hook: A study of ~600,000 U.S. veterans links GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide to lower rates of addiction and overdose — an association, not proof that the drugs cause the effect.

related.title: Ozempic Linked to Fewer Bone Fractures
related.hook: Losing weight often costs you bone. Yet a study of nearly 60,000 people with type 2 diabetes found semaglutide users had about 15% fewer fractures — even though they lost more weight.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of hair loss did the GLP-1 study find more of — and why does the type matter?

choices.text: Non-scarring alopecia, where the follicle survives, so hair can regrow
Scarring alopecia, which destroys the follicle permanently
Complete, irreversible baldness in most users

flashcards.explanation_html: The excess risk was in non-scarring alopecia. Because the follicle stays intact, this form is potentially reversible — a meaningfully different prospect from scarring hair loss.

flashcards.prompt: How big is the hair-loss risk on GLP-1 drugs in absolute terms?
flashcards.back_html: Small. Roughly 6.9 cases per 1,000 person-years on a GLP-1 versus 5.0 on an SGLT-2 inhibitor — a 37% relative increase on top of an already low baseline.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't this study prove the drug itself causes the hair loss?
flashcards.back_html: It's observational — it compares people who happened to be prescribed different drugs. GLP-1 users were younger and heavier, and rapid weight loss on its own can trigger shedding, so the drug and its effect are hard to separate.
